10/ But at least we should be clear that's the bet we're making, and stop pretending that Bezos is Scrooge McDuck.

9/ We're all placing a collective bet that worldchanging innovations that the betting economy might encourage will make us richer faster than the lost bets impoverish us. It might be a good bet, or it might not.
8/ In many ways QE is a 2nd mortgage on our collective future, so you could make the case that Bezos and other stock market billionaires are borrowing their wealth from all of us.
7/ Bezos also forgot to thank the Federal Reserve and other central banks for Quantitative Easing, which has flooded the world with capital, helping keep stock prices so high!
6/ I explained this idea recently using a different billionaire as the case study in https://t.co/4O8dLaQin9

5/ It comes from an entirely different economy, which I call the Supermoney economy, in which people with too much capital to get the returns they want in the operating economy try to get outsized returns in the betting economy.
4/ Amazon's stock price is only loosely correlated with its profits.
3/ I've done the math, multiplying Amazon's profit each year since IPO by his percentage ownership, which has declined from 41% at IPO to 11% today as he has sold or otherwise disposed of shares.
2/ Bezos doesn't personally get to keep Amazon's profits, and if he did,  he'd be worth only about $6 billion, not the $200+ billion he has today.

1/ It's also the case that @jeffbezos forgot to thank the people bidding up the price of Amazon's stock. Everyone seems to ignore that his wealth comes from Amazon stock sales, not from his personal share of Amazon's profits.

11/ I probably shouldn't have hijacked this brilliant paper on what's wrong with military innovation to talk about what's wrong with Silicon Valley funding. It's an important read on what's wrong with government (not just the military). Very insightful.

10/ So many people had identified outdated government procurement rules as the problem, but it's really congressional budgeting.

So too, many of the failures ahead will not be failures of the entrepreneurial ideas. They will be failures of capital allocation.

9/ As one wise friend of mine said, "We're just debating whether it is 1997 or 1999."

The @HudsonInstitute report is worth studying, because it highlights the way that funding shapes markets more than virtually any other factor.

8/ It is impossible to predict when the investment tide will go out, but there are certainly signs that it may be starting to turn. While I'm sure some solid companies will go public via SPAC, the current mania reminds me all too well of the later days of the dotcom boom.

7/ When startups are valued at billions before they've proven their business model, trouble lies ahead. I suspect that we're coming to a moment of reckoning for many companies. As Warren Buffet once said, "You never know who's swimming naked until the tide goes out."

6/ We like to tell ourselves that companies can pivot, but the constraints on a company that has raised too much money are extreme. Rather than learning as it goes, it has to go all in on winner-takes-all growth, which may be unsustainable.
5/ Raising an enormous amount of capital before you've learned what works is a lot like what the military does: commit a huge budget to a plan despite fundamental uncertainty.
4/ Silicon Valley funding used to be completely in step with that lean startup model. Unfortunately, the current stage of Silicon Valley investing seems to have lost the plot.

3/ The deepest innovation of Silicon Valley companies is not a specific technology or set of technologies that can be taken out of context and pasted into an old organization. In many ways, it is an approach to solving problems iteratively, learning as you go.

2/ You can't get to new outcomes without changing the processes that you use to achieve them. New technology is not independent of culture, business processes, and the skills of the people you ask to implement it. And maybe even more importantly, how it is funded.

@kevinmarks @AOC There is a host of sins for which the tech companies are responsible. We need to make sure we accuse them of the things that are their actual problem.

@kevinmarks @AOC If you want to solve a problem, you have to diagnose it correctly. Calling it “selling data” gives companies a huge out, since they don’t actually sell the data. The question is whether these company’s use customer data for their benefit or against them.

@kevinmarks @AOC And the idea that people don’t consent to having their data used to target ads for an ad-supported service seems a bit far-fetched. People don’t understand how much data is available, and how intrusive it can be, but that’s not the same thing.
@kevinmarks @AOC Can you show me an example of where Twitter, Facebook, and Google sell data? Ad targeting is not selling data.
@edkohler @AOC Yes, that’s right.

@benjiedlp @AOC Yes, Cambridge Analytica - got its data through Facebook’s developer program, designed to let 3rd parties build apps on Facebook. The data was not sold. I stand by my statement that Google and FB don’t sell user data. They use it in their business.

@AOC I love you and what you stand up for, but you are wrong on this. The tech platforms have business models that use your data to deliver services and ads to you, but they do not resell your data to others. The ones who do that are banks, credit card companies, and telcos.

@pomeranian99 @Uber @lyft Right, but by being clear that a) you’ll make good money at these times, and b) you’ll earn bubkus at these, you would use price signaling to encourage or discourage that pool. There are other data signals besides price that they could have used to discourage drivers too.

@JMarkOckerbloom It’s worth remembering that both Sidecar (Sunil Paul’s original company, which invented the model) and the early Lyft, worked with regulators. And lost to Uber by it. And also that Uber was right that most of the regulations were protectionist regulatory-capture by incumbents.

@pomeranian99 One mistake that @uber and @lyft made was in over-promising to draw the most drivers, rather than optimizing for that part-time peak. They should have been discouraging drivers at other times, to keep earnings up. A hard optimization problem, but I don’t think they even tried.

@pomeranian99 I’m not sure that cab fleets could have done it, except in the densest cities. It isn’t just the GPS matching. It is the on-demand drivers and surge pricing to bring more drivers into the market to meet peak demand. Most cab companies don’t have enough for peak.

@pomeranian99 Yeah, that bothered me. This was a real innovation, though it would likely have developed in a more healthy way in the absence of the winner-takes-all race, which was the point I made in my blitzscaling piece.

That is to say, the problem is not with @uber or @lyft per se, or with the technology (which is far from as thin as the authors pretend), but with the financial incentives that our current stock market mania provides. Let’s fix that, and start valuing “real companies” again.

If @uber and @lyft hadn’t been treated as financial instruments rather than companies, they would have grown more slowly, there would have been more competition, and the companies would have had to discover the right balance between rewarding drivers and rewarding passengers.

The problem is the financial model that shoots for the stock price rather than an operating business as the real target, leads the company to value growth over profits, thus squeezing the drivers for profitability while continuing to subsidize riders.

That being said, I think that the American Affairs is too negative on the possibility of these companies achieving profitability. If you take out the enormous amount spent on hype-driven R&D, and on growth marketing and passenger subsidies, drivers could take more of the pie.
